turns.prompt_text: what kind of trackers do you eat rabbit wear
turns.response_html:
When tracking wild rabbits like the New England cottontails released today, biologists have to be incredibly careful. Rabbits are small, fast, and often hide underground, which makes traditional bulky tracking gear impossible to use.

Depending on the specific goal of the study, researchers usually use one of three types of technology:

1. Micro-GPS Collars (The "High-Tech" Choice)

For the recent releases, many rabbits are fitted with Nano-GPS collars.

  • Featherweight: These devices are tiny, weighing as little as 10 to 12 grams (about the weight of two or three nickels) so they don't hinder the rabbit’s speed or ability to squeeze into thickets.
  • Smart Features: Because rabbits spend so much time in underground burrows where GPS signals can't reach, the trackers are programmed with "Smart GPS." They only turn on when the rabbit is moving and outdoors, which saves battery life.
  • Remote Downloads: Biologists don't have to catch the rabbit again to get the data; the collar can beam its location history to a handheld receiver or a base station from up to 500 meters away.

2. VHF Radio Collars (The "Traditional" Choice)

These are the most common for long-term survival monitoring.

  • The Signal: They emit a simple "beep" on a specific radio frequency.
  • Manual Tracking: A volunteer or biologist walks through the brush with a directional antenna (which looks like an old-school TV antenna). As they get closer to the rabbit, the beeping gets louder.
  • Mortality Sensors: These have a clever feature: if the rabbit doesn't move for several hours, the "beep" pattern changes. This tells researchers immediately if a rabbit has been lost to a predator or illness.

3. The "Non-Invasive" Tracker (DNA)

Sometimes, the best "tracker" isn't a device at all. Because New England cottontails are so secretive, scientists often track them through DNA pellet surveys.

  • By collecting rabbit droppings (pellets) in the snow, researchers can identify exactly which individual rabbit was there without ever having to touch or stress the animal. This is how they estimate population growth across large areas like Maine and New Hampshire.

Did you know? To keep the rabbits safe, the collars are designed to be perfectly smooth and "thread-free" on the inside. This prevents the fur from matting or the skin from getting irritated as the rabbit moves through dense thorns and briars.

turns.prompt_text: I need to put microchips on a many many different hardware tools
turns.response_html:
When it comes to "microchipping" hardware tools, the approach is a bit different than the grain-of-rice chips used for pets. Because tools are often made of metal (which blocks signals) and endure heavy vibration, you’ll want to choose a solution based on how many tools you have and how far away you need to track them.

Here is a breakdown of the best "chipping" methods for a hardware inventory, ranging from simple organization to high-tech anti-theft.

1. Bluetooth Tags (The "Smart" Choice for Power Tools)

If you have high-value items like drills, saws, or specialized kits, Bluetooth trackers are the standard. They act like a "Tile" or "AirTag" but are ruggedized for job sites.

  • The Big Players: * Milwaukee TICK: A small, weather-proof disc you screw, glue, or rivet onto any tool. It syncs with the One-Key app.
    • DeWalt Tool Connect: Small chips that can be glued into specific slots on newer DeWalt tools or adhered to the outside of others.
  • Pros: Shows you the "last seen" location on a map; can "ping" the tool to find it under a pile of rubble; high-tech anti-theft (some can be remotely disabled).
  • Cons: Requires a battery (usually lasts 1–3 years) and is too bulky for small hand tools like screwdrivers or pliers.

2. NFC/RFID Tags (The "Bulk" Inventory Choice)

If you have "many, many" tools (hundreds of hand tools, sockets, or wrenches), you likely want Passive RFID or NFC tags. These are the closest thing to a "microchip."

  • How it works: You stick a small, flat "button" or "laundry tag" onto the tool. It has no battery. You scan it with your phone or a handheld reader.
  • Industrial Strength: Look for "On-Metal" RFID tags. Regular stickers won't work on metal tools because the metal interferes with the antenna; "on-metal" tags have a small foam or ceramic spacer to solve this.
  • Pros: Very cheap (often less than $1 per tag); no batteries to replace; tiny enough for almost any tool.
  • Cons: Short range. You usually have to be within a few inches (NFC) or a few feet (UHF RFID) to "read" the chip.

3. Smart Asset ID Tags (The Modern Barcode)

Companies like Milwaukee and Hilti now sell "Asset ID" tags that are highly durable stickers with a unique QR code and a hidden internal ID.

  • The Benefit: They are designed to withstand grease, chemicals, and abrasion. Even if the QR code gets scratched, the "chip" inside can often still be read by a scanner.
  • Best For: Creating a digital "check-out" system for a crew or a large workshop.

Comparison Table: Which "Chip" is Right for You?

FeatureBluetooth (TICK/Link)RFID/NFC ButtonsQR/Asset ID Tags
Best ForExpensive Power ToolsHand Tools/Large KitsGeneral Inventory
Tracking RangeUp to 100+ feet1 inch to 10 feetLine of sight
Battery?Yes (1–3 years)NoNo
Cost~$20–$30 per tool~$0.50–$2.00 per tool~$1.00 per tag
AttachmentScrew, Rivet, EpoxyAdhesiveIndustrial Adhesive

Pro-Tip: The "Glue" Matters

For hardware tools, the sticker itself is rarely enough. Most pros use two-part epoxy (like JB Weld) to encase the chip or tag onto the tool. This ensures it doesn't pop off when the tool vibrates or gets dropped.

Milwaukee Tool Tracking Options

While the standard TICK focuses purely on tracking, Milwaukee recently updated their lineup with a "Tracking Tag" that includes an audible speaker to help you find tools in the dark or under debris, though it still lacks a light.

  • Milwaukee TICK Tool and Equipment Tracker: This is the classic ruggedized "chip." It is built to survive extreme job site conditions (water, dust, and impact) and has a 1-year replaceable battery. It is best for discreetly mounting to heavy machinery or ladders.
  • Milwaukee ONE-KEY Bluetooth Tracking Tag: A more modern version with a 300-foot range and a built-in speaker. While it doesn't have a flashlight, you can "ring" the tag from your phone to locate it by sound.

If the flashlight is a must-have feature for your hardware tools or keychain, these alternatives integrate both technologies:

Milwaukee TICK & Bluetooth Tag

The Milwaukee TICK is the original heavy-duty tracker. It’s designed to be a "set it and forget it" beacon for everything from ladders to job boxes. Pro-Tip for Attachment: For metal tools, avoid using just the adhesive backing. Use a two-part epoxy or pop-rivets through the mounting holes. This prevents the tag from being knocked off during heavy use or intentionally removed by someone else.

turns.prompt_text: for the Bluetooth stick/link are there any online schematics that can be sent to pcbway to have them mass-produced it
turns.response_html:
To mass-produce Bluetooth trackers via a service like PCBWay, you don't need to reinvent the wheel. Since commercial brands like Milwaukee or DeWalt keep their schematics private, the best way forward is to use Open Source Hardware (OSHW) designs.

There are several "ready-to-manufacture" projects specifically designed for low-cost, high-volume production.

1. The Best "Mass-Production Ready" Design: Tiny BLE Beacon

On PCBWay's own "Shared Projects" platform, there is a design called the Tiny BLE Beacon (11x11mm).

  • The Schematic: It uses the CH591D microcontroller, which is incredibly cheap (often under $0.50 in bulk).
  • Form Factor: At 11mm, it is small enough to be embedded inside the plastic housing of a drill or epoxied into the handle of a hand tool.
  • Production: You can directly "Add to Cart" on PCBWay, or download the Gerber files and Bill of Materials (BOM) to customize it.

2. The "Industry Standard" Design: nRF52832 Beacons

If you want your trackers to work with a wide variety of apps (like Apple's "Find My" or generic Bluetooth scanners), look for designs based on the Nordic nRF52832 chip.

  • Where to find files: Search GitHub for "nRF52832 Beacon Gerber."
  • Why use this: This chip is the gold standard for low-power Bluetooth. There are hundreds of open-source PCB layouts available that are already optimized for CR2032 coin cell batteries, which can power a tool tracker for 1–2 years.
  • Reliability: These designs are "tried and true," meaning the antenna layout (the hardest part of a Bluetooth PCB) is already proven to work.

3. How to Order from PCBWay for Your Tools

When you send these schematics to PCBWay, you should request Turnkey PCB Assembly. This means they buy the chips, print the boards, and solder everything for you.

StepAction for Mass Production
FilesUpload the Gerber files (the board map) and the BOM (list of parts).
StencilRequest a "Solder Stencil" for the tiny Bluetooth chips.
BatteryAsk them to include a Battery Clip (for CR2032) or a Solder Tab for a permanent battery.
EnclosureSince these are for tools, you may want to ask for Conformal Coating—this is a thin waterproof film sprayed over the electronics to protect them from dust and oil in your workshop.

The "Pro" Shortcut: Wiliot IoT Pixels

If "mass-produced" means you need thousands of these, you might look into Wiliot. They produce "battery-free" Bluetooth stickers (IoT Pixels) that harvest energy from the air. You don't even need a PCB; they are as thin as a shipping label and can be stuck directly onto tools.

Important Consideration: The Case

A bare PCB will break immediately on a job site. If you produce these, you will also need a 3D-printed or injection-molded housing.

turns.prompt_text: please tell me more about these iot pixels
turns.response_html:
Wiliot’s IoT Pixels are a massive shift in how hardware can be tracked because they essentially turn every tool into a smart device without needing a battery. Think of them as a "bridge" between a standard barcode (which is cheap but "dumb") and a high-end GPS tracker (which is "smart" but expensive and bulky).

Here is a deeper look at how they work and how you can use them for your "many, many tools."

1. How They Work (The "Magic" Part)

These are "Ambient IoT" devices. They don't have a battery; instead, they have a tiny antenna that harvests energy from the radio waves already in the air (from Wi-Fi routers, other Bluetooth devices, or specialized "PowerBridges").

  • Size: They are the size of a postage stamp (2.8 x 4.4 cm) and about as thin as a sticker (0.2mm).
  • Intelligence: Despite their size, they contain an ARM Cortex processor. They can sense location, temperature, and even movement (they can tell if a tool is being picked up or vibrating).
  • Communication: They broadcast a standard Bluetooth beacon that can be picked up by any smartphone or Bluetooth gateway.

2. Why They Are Better for Mass Tool Tracking

If you have a warehouse or a large workshop full of tools, IoT Pixels offer several advantages over traditional methods:

  • Cost: In high volume, these can cost as little as $0.10 to $0.20 per tag.
  • Zero Maintenance: Since there are no batteries, you never have to go through your hundreds of tools to "recharge" or swap batteries. They have a lifespan of over a decade.
  • Scan-Free: Unlike barcodes or standard RFID, you don't have to walk up to each tool and scan it. If the tool is within range of a "Bridge" or your phone, it simply "checks itself in" to your digital inventory.

3. The Infrastructure You’ll Need

Because these tags harvest energy, they need a "source" to wake them up. To track "many, many" tools in a specific area (like an Ankeny workshop or a job site trailer), you would set up:

  • PowerBridges: These are small plug-in devices (often look like Wi-Fi extenders) that "bathe" the room in radio energy. This wakes up the tags on your tools.
  • The Wiliot Cloud: The tags send encrypted data to the cloud, where an AI analyzes it. For example, it can alert you if a tool hasn't moved in 30 days or if it’s currently in a location it shouldn't be.

4. How to Apply Them to Hardware

Since your tools are likely metal and subject to rough handling, you can't just slap a paper sticker on them. To use IoT Pixels for hardware:

  • Encapsulation: You can buy these embedded in plastic "hard tags" or "on-metal" versions.
  • Embedding: If you are a tool manufacturer (or doing a DIY version), you can actually embed the Pixel sticker inside the handle of a tool or under a plastic guard during assembly. Because it's so thin, it doesn't change the tool's ergonomics.

How to Get Started

If you want to move away from the PCBWay custom-build route and use this ready-made technology:

  1. Starter Kits: Wiliot sells "Starter Kits" that include a handful of Pixels and a Bridge so you can test the range in your specific workshop.
  2. On-Metal Spacers: If you are sticking them to metal wrenches or drills, make sure to get the versions designed for metal surfaces, as metal normally "shorts out" the energy-harvesting antenna.

Wiliot’s IoT Pixels are essentially "smart stickers" that act like a tiny computer without a battery. Because they harvest energy from radio waves (like Wi-Fi and Bluetooth) in the air, they can last for years without maintenance.

Here is the breakdown of the cost and how you would actually apply them to your hardware:

1. Getting Started: The Cost

Wiliot has moved from working only with massive corporations to offering a Starter Kit for smaller developers and businesses.

  • Price: Approximately $500.
  • What’s Inside: Typically includes one "Bridge" (the device that provides energy to the tags), several IoT Pixels (single and dual-band stickers), and a 6-month subscription to their cloud platform where you track the data.
  • Mass Production Cost: While the kit is for testing, the tags themselves are designed to cost "pennies" in high volume (aiming for under $0.10–$0.20 per tag).

2. How to Apply Them to Tools

Since your tools are likely metal and subject to heavy use, you can't just stick a paper label on them. Here is the industrial approach:

  • The "On-Metal" Problem: Metal surfaces reflect radio waves and can "short out" the antenna on a standard sticker. To fix this, you use On-Metal Tags. These have a thin layer of foam or plastic built into the sticker to create a gap between the chip and the metal.
  • Encapsulation (Hard Tags): For hammers, drills, or wrenches, you can buy these pixels already embedded inside rugged plastic housings. These can be riveted, screwed, or glued with industrial epoxy to the tool.
  • Embedding: If you are building your own hardware or have tools with plastic handles, you can actually hide the pixel inside the plastic housing during assembly. Because they are only 0.2mm thick, they don't affect the shape of the tool.

3. Technical Specs for Your Inventory

  • Range: About 10 meters (30 feet). This is perfect for a workshop or a tool trailer. If a tool leaves that 10-meter bubble around a "Bridge," the system will mark it as "Checked Out" or "Missing."
  • Sensing: Beyond just ID tracking, these pixels can detect temperature and movement. For example, the system could alert you if a sensitive laser level is being stored in a freezing truck or if a tool is vibrating (meaning it's currently in use).
  • Security: They use 128-bit AES encryption, so someone can't easily "clone" your tool's ID to bypass your inventory system.

4. Where to Buy

You can purchase the starter kits directly through Wiliot’s website or through industrial partners like Avnet or Identiv.

The Workflow for You:

  1. Order the Starter Kit to test the signal strength in your specific shop.
  2. Tag your tools using the "on-metal" adhesive versions or by epoxying the stickers onto flat surfaces.
  3. Plug in a Bridge in your workshop.
  4. Open the App: Every time you walk into the shop, your phone or the bridge will "wake up" the tools, and you’ll see a real-time list of everything that is present.
